consensus_summary: All three blind responses agree the phrase in Matthew 12:40 refers to Jesus' death-and-burial interval: primarily the tomb/grave, often extended to Sheol/Hades (the realm of the dead), fulfilling the Jonah typology of three days and nights before resurrection. The Jerusalem/'heart of the land' reading is noted only as a minority or rare alternative.
book_summary: The book identifies 'the heart of the earth' as Jerusalem itself — the navel and heart of the land — citing Ezekiel 5:5 and 38:12 where Jerusalem is set 'in the midst of the nations' and 'in the midst of the land.' It explicitly labels the grave/Hades reading as the merely 'commonly taught' view.
consensus_core_identification: The tomb/grave (and by traditional extension Sheol/Hades) where Christ lay between his death and resurrection.
book_core_identification: Jerusalem, the geographic and covenantal center ('navel/heart') of the land, as the place where the Son of Man spent three days and three nights.
boundary_disagreement: The book's reading implicitly shifts the three-days-and-nights period: if 'heart of the earth' means Jerusalem, the count can begin with Jesus' arrest/custody in the city rather than with burial, reclassifying the fulfillment window. The consensus ties the period strictly to the death-to-resurrection interval in the tomb/underworld.
material_contradiction: The book says 'heart of the earth' names Jerusalem (a city on the surface of the land); the consensus says it names the grave or the subterranean realm of the dead. These cannot both be the referent of the same phrase in the same verse and sense. The book's own common-view note ('Commonly taught: the grave or Hades') signals deliberate rejection and replacement of the consensus identification.
rationale: Both consensus responses A and B list the Jerusalem/'heart of the land' reading, but only as a minority or rare alternative — the settled core is the tomb/Hades. The book elevates that minority reading to its primary identification and explicitly frames the grave/Hades view as the merely common teaching it departs from. Since accepting Jerusalem as the referent requires rejecting the tomb/Hades identification (not merely narrowing or sharpening it), this is DIVERGENT rather than REFINED, even though the reading is recognizable within the alternatives list (NOVEL does not apply because the reading is known to the consensus responses).
strongest_objection: The Ezekiel texts establish that Jerusalem sits 'in the midst' of the nations/land, but neither uses the phrase 'heart of the earth,' and Matthew 12:40's Jonah parallel (Jonah in the fish's belly, crying from 'the belly of Sheol,' Jonah 2:2) more naturally maps to confinement in death/the grave than to presence in a city. Jesus was also demonstrably in Jerusalem before and after the three days, which strains the specific temporal fit that the tomb reading satisfies; the printed citations alone do not overcome this typological objection.
